overview.title: 📖 Overview: Habits, Lice, and Bedside Manners
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 12a–12b
overview.hebrewSource: שַׁבָּת הִיא מִלִּזְעוֹק וּרְפוּאָה קְרוֹבָה לָבֹא
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf resolves the contradiction about a zav's pouch, then works through several of the mishna's Shabbat-eve precautions in detail. Unlike the tailor's needle, tefillin may be worn out at dusk because a person is obligated to keep feeling them. The Gemara analyzes killing lice, delousing clothing in public, and reading by the light of a lamp — including how far the Sages' concern about adjusting the wick extends. It closes with the halakhot and etiquette of comforting mourners and visiting the sick on Shabbat, a leniency the Sages permitted only with difficulty.

slides.title: 🕯️ Reading by Candlelight — How Far Does the Decree Reach?
slides.subtitle: Rabba, the bonfire case, and an exception for an important person

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabba: the ban applies even if the lamp is two stories high, or ten houses stacked one atop another — height gives no leniency, since it is a flat decree
2️⃣ One person may not read alone; but two together, engaged in the same matter, may — since they remind each other. Engaged in two different matters, even two may not
3️⃣ Around a bonfire (Rav Huna), even ten people seated apart may not read, since no one notices another adjusting the coals

4️⃣ Rava: an important person may read, since he would never personally touch a dirty lamp — yet Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha, who treated himself as a commoner for Torah, nearly adjusted the wick anyway, and (per Rabbi Natan) recorded the act in his notebook to bring a sin-offering when the Temple is rebuilt

slides.title: 😷 Weekday Kindnesses on Shabbat
slides.subtitle: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute matchmaking, teaching, mourning, and sick-visits

boxes.title: Beit Shammai forbids
items: Arranging a match to betroth children
Committing a child to learn Torah or a trade
— these are weekday matters, out of place on Shabbat

boxes.title: Beit Hillel permits
items: All of the above — since each act includes an element of mitzva

boxes.title: Still, a caution (R' Ḥanina)
items: 'Only with great difficulty did they permit comforting mourners and visiting the sick on Shabbat' — both visitor and mourner feel pain in the act

slides.title: 🗣️ What to Say at a Sick Person's Bedside
slides.subtitle: Several formulas, all built around 'Shabbat is here, from crying out'
rows: 'It is Shabbat, when one may not cry out, and healing is soon to come'
Adds: 'Shabbat's merit is capable of engendering compassion'
'May the Omnipresent have compassion on you and on all the sick of Israel'
'...on you, among the sick of Israel' — including him within the community
Says shalom on entering; on leaving, the full formula plus 'His compassion is abundant, rest in peace'

callout.label: Where to sit:
callout.text: One should sit neither on the bed nor on a chair, but wrap himself and sit before the patient, since the Divine Presence rests above the sick person's head (Psalms 41:4, 'God will support him on the bed of illness').

slides.title: 🪱 Killing a Louse on Shabbat
slides.subtitle: From Rabbi Eliezer's severity to Rav Huna's practical ruling

nodes.content: ❓ Rabbi Eliezer: one who kills a louse on Shabbat is as though he killed a camel
⚖️ Beit Shammai forbid killing a louse on Shabbat; Beit Hillel permit it

columns.label: Tosefta
columns.content: May squeeze the louse and throw it away, but not kill it outright

columns.label: Abba Shaul
columns.content: May take and throw it, but not squeeze it — in his view killing a louse is Torah-forbidden

nodes.content: ✅ Rav Huna: the halakha is squeeze and throw — the dignified way, even on weekdays. (Rabba and Rav Sheshet simply killed lice; Rava threw them into water; Rav Naḥman told his daughters, 'kill them, and let me hear the sound of the combs')

slides.title: 🧣 Tefillin at Dusk — Unlike the Tailor's Needle
slides.subtitle: A kal vaḥomer from the High Priest's frontplate

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: A person may go out with tefillin on Shabbat eve at nightfall, ab initio — unlike the tailor's needle or scribe's quill.

lines.speaker: Why?
lines.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna: a person must constantly touch his tefillin — a kal vaḥomer from the High Priest's frontplate (tzitz), which has only one mention of God's name yet the Torah says must never leave his awareness (Exodus 28:38).

lines.speaker: Result
lines.text: Tefillin carry many more mentions of God's name, so one certainly remains aware of them and is unlikely to carry them out absentmindedly.

lines.speaker: Ḥananya
lines.text: adds a related practice: feel your clothing at dusk on Shabbat eve to check you haven't forgotten something in your pockets — Rav Yosef called this 'a significant halakha for Shabbat.'

summary.principle: The Sages' Shabbat-eve precautions were finely tuned: some objects, like the tailor's needle, are restricted because habit makes forgetting likely, while tefillin are exempted precisely because a person is obligated to stay constantly aware of them.

flowSteps.content: 🧣 Tefillin permitted at dusk — a person must always feel them (kal vaḥomer from the tzitz)
🪱 Killing lice: Beit Shammai forbid, Beit Hillel permit; Rav Huna rules 'squeeze and throw'

columns.content: 😷 Beit Hillel permits matchmaking, teaching, comforting mourners, and visiting the sick — each holds a mitzva
🕯️ Reading by candlelight stays forbidden regardless of height, except for an important person

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: These leniencies for the sick and mourning were granted, in R' Ḥanina's words, 'only with great difficulty'

quiz.q: Why is a person permitted to go out with tefillin on Shabbat eve at dusk, unlike a tailor with his needle?
o: Tefillin are too light to count as carrying
A person is obligated to constantly feel his tefillin, so he is unlikely to forget them and carry them out absentmindedly
Tefillin may only be worn during the day anyway
The mishna never mentions tefillin at all
quiz.e: Rabba bar Rav Huna derived by a kal vaḥomer from the High Priest's frontplate that a person must always keep his tefillin in mind, so there is no concern he will forget and carry them into the public domain.

quiz.q: According to Beit Hillel, why may one arrange a match for children, teach a child a trade, comfort mourners, or visit the sick on Shabbat, against Beit Shammai's view that these are weekday matters?
o: Because Beit Hillel does not believe in observing Shabbat restrictions
Because each of these acts includes an element of mitzva
Because Shabbat has no bearing on interpersonal conduct
Because Beit Shammai's ruling was later overturned by a vote
quiz.e: Beit Hillel permits these activities specifically because each one carries a mitzva element, which overrides the concern that they are ordinarily weekday pursuits.

quiz.q: According to the baraita, where should a person sit when visiting someone who is sick, and why?
o: On the patient's bed, to comfort him directly
On a chair facing the patient
Neither on the bed nor a chair, but wrapped and seated before the patient, since the Divine Presence rests above his head
Standing at the doorway only
quiz.e: The baraita teaches that one should sit neither on the bed nor a chair but wrap himself and sit before the sick person, since the Divine Presence is above the patient's head (Psalms 41:4).

quiz.q: What is Rav Huna's practical ruling about dealing with lice found on Shabbat?
o: One must always crush them immediately
One should squeeze the louse and throw it away — the dignified method, even on weekdays
One may not touch lice at all, even to remove them
One must burn the garment containing them
quiz.e: Rav Huna ruled that the halakha follows squeezing and throwing the louse, calling this the dignified way to handle it, applicable even during the week.

quiz.q: According to Rabba, does raising a candle out of reach (e.g. two stories high) permit reading by its light on Shabbat?
o: Yes, once it is out of reach the concern no longer applies
No — the decree applies regardless of height, even ten houses stacked atop one another
Only if it is exactly one story high
Only for an important person
quiz.e: Rabba ruled that the prohibition against reading by candlelight applies no matter how high the lamp is placed, since the decree was issued flatly rather than tied to actual reach.
